title: SIU death investigation 'enraged' victim's family
subtitle: A mother is trying to sue the SIU after she found out they didn't question the police officer who shot her 15-year-old son.
article: Simone Wellington was jolted by a gunshot coming from the parking lot of her Scarborough apartment building early one morning in June 2006.
What she didn't know was that police had just killed her 15-year-old son, Duane Christian, who had been driving a stolen van.
"I heard it," said Wellington, who cooperated with a probe by the province's Special Investigations Unit and expected credible answers to why her son was killed.

But then Wellington discovered the SIU didn't bother interviewing the officer who fired the fatal shot, Const. Steve Darnley, and had cleared police of wrongdoing before receiving a report from an autopsy.

Wellington and her daughter, Alexis, filed a negligence lawsuit against the SIU, relying on a 2007 decision from the Supreme Court of Canada that opened the door to lawsuits against police for incompetent criminal investigations.

Since then, the Crown and the Ontario Association of Chiefs of Police have been marshalling some of their finest legal talent in an attempt to stop the case from proceeding. The issue: can victims' families sue police for sloppy investigations or does that right only belong to people charged?

The latest stop was the Ontario Court of Appeal. On Tuesday, a judge pressed Wellington's lawyer to explain why he encouraged her to pursue a novel claim that's likely to result in minimal damages and threatens to turn into a public inquiry into the SIU, especially when a more conventional remedy - a civil lawsuit for damages - could be a faster route to getting answers.
"I don't know why in the world you would want to go off on this garden path," Justice Robert Armstrong told Peter Rosenthal, the family's lawyer.
"That's not what justice is about for this family," he suggested. "Justice is about getting them to court and getting an answer."
But Rosenthal said the way the SIU handled the investigation made Wellington feel as though her son "was worthless."
"To be honest with you, sir," he told the judge, "I will tell you that my client was enraged by the SIU investigation."
Crown counsel Lise Favreau argued the Wellingtons have no basis for a negligence claim because the SIU in these circumstances owes no private duty of care to families of police shooting victims.

But Justice Michael Moldaver suggested allowing families to sue could further the integrity of these investigations and ensure officers and SIU investigators are not "playing footsie" with one another.

On the other hand, said Justice Robert Sharpe, there is also the question of whether SIU officers should have the threat of lawsuits from disappointed family members "hanging over their heads" while they conduct their investigations - and whether this could lead to them laying charges even in weak cases, leaving it to the courts to sort things out.
As to whether Wellington's lawsuit can proceed, the appeal panel reserved its decision.
